questions.q: Under Muslim law, marriage (Nikah) is fundamentally regarded as:
o: A religious sacrament, exactly like Hindu marriage
A CIVIL CONTRACT, requiring offer, acceptance, and consideration in the form of Mahr
An arrangement with no legal significance whatsoever
Valid only if registered with the government
questions.src: Muslim marriage is fundamentally contractual in nature, distinguishing it from the sacramental view traditionally associated with Hindu marriage.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the four traditional sources of Muslim law?
o: Quran
Sunna/Hadith
Ijma (consensus)
Custom alone, independent of the other sources
questions.src: The four traditional sources are Quran, Sunna, Ijma, and Qiyas — custom alone is not an independent primary source in the traditional classification.

questions.q: A "Fasid" (irregular) marriage under Muslim law is best distinguished from a "Batil" (void) marriage by the fact that:
o: They are legally identical in every respect
A Fasid marriage has a removable defect and children born are legitimate; a Batil marriage has NO legal effect at all and violates an absolute prohibition
Batil marriages are always valid, while Fasid marriages are never valid
Only Fasid marriages require a formal divorce to end
questions.src: Fasid marriages have removable defects with legitimate children; Batil marriages are void ab initio with no legal effect, violating absolute prohibitions like consanguinity.

questions.q: "Muta" marriage — a temporary marriage for a fixed duration — is recognised:
o: Under both Sunni and Shia law equally
ONLY under Shia (Ithna Ashari) law, not under Sunni law
Only under Sunni law
Nowhere in Muslim law
questions.src: Muta marriage is a distinctive feature of Shia law only, automatically terminating upon expiry of the specified term.

questions.q: "Mahr" (dower) under Muslim law is:
o: The husband's exclusive property
The WIFE'S exclusive property, payable/settled by the husband as an essential incident of marriage
Property jointly owned by both spouses
A payment made by the wife to the husband
questions.src: Mahr is the wife's own exclusive property — a financial right belonging to her, not subject to the husband's control.

questions.q: "Prompt Dower" (Mu'ajjal), as distinguished from "Deferred Dower," is:
o: Payable only upon the husband's death
Payable on demand, at any time before or after consummation
Never actually payable under any circumstances
Only applicable to second marriages
questions.src: Prompt dower is payable immediately on the wife's demand, giving her the right to refuse cohabitation until it is paid.

questions.q: If a Muslim marriage is dissolved BEFORE consummation, the wife is generally entitled to:
o: No dower whatsoever
HALF of the specified dower
Full dower plus additional compensation
Only deferred dower, never prompt dower
questions.src: Dissolution before consummation entitles the wife to half the specified dower; dissolution after consummation entitles her to the full amount.

questions.q: "Talaq-e-Ahsan," considered the most approved form of divorce, involves:
o: Three pronouncements made in a single sitting
A SINGLE pronouncement made during a Tuhr, followed by the Iddat period, revocable throughout Iddat
No pronouncement at all, only mutual silence
A pronouncement that takes effect instantly with no waiting period
questions.src: Talaq-e-Ahsan is a single pronouncement during a period of purity (Tuhr), remaining revocable throughout the subsequent Iddat period.

questions.q: "Talaq-e-Biddat" (triple talaq), as declared in Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017), is:
o: Constitutionally valid and still legally recognised
UNCONSTITUTIONAL — struck down by a 3:2 Supreme Court majority as manifestly arbitrary
Only valid if performed in writing
A form recognised exclusively under Shia law
questions.src: Shayara Bano declared talaq-e-biddat unconstitutional; the subsequent 2019 Act made pronouncing it a criminal offence.

questions.q: Following the Shayara Bano judgment, Parliament enacted which legislation to criminalise talaq-e-biddat?
o: The Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act 1939
The Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act 2019
The Hindu Marriage Act 1955
The Special Marriage Act 1954
questions.src: The 2019 Act made pronouncing talaq-e-biddat a criminal offence, punishable with imprisonment up to 3 years.

questions.q: "Khula" as a form of divorce under Muslim law refers to:
o: Divorce initiated unilaterally by the husband alone
Divorce initiated BY THE WIFE, with the husband's consent, typically involving her relinquishing her dower claim
A divorce that can never actually be finalised
Divorce granted only by a court, never by the parties themselves
questions.src: Khula is wife-initiated divorce, requiring the husband's consent, generally in exchange for the wife giving up her dower or other consideration.

questions.q: In Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum (1985), the Supreme Court held that Section 125 CrPC (secular maintenance provision):
o: Does not apply to Muslim women at all
Applies to Muslim women exactly as to women of any other faith, and is NOT automatically limited to the Iddat period
Applies only during the marriage, never after divorce
Was struck down as unconstitutional in this case
questions.src: Shah Bano established that the secular Section 125 CrPC maintenance right is not confined to Iddat merely because of Muslim Personal Law.

questions.q: The Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986 was enacted:
o: Before the Shah Bano judgment, unrelated to it
In apparent response to the Shah Bano judgment, seemingly limiting maintenance to the Iddat period on its face
To abolish all maintenance rights for Muslim women entirely
To extend Hindu Marriage Act provisions to Muslims
questions.src: The 1986 Act followed political controversy after Shah Bano, appearing to restrict maintenance obligations to the Iddat period.

questions.q: In Danial Latifi v. Union of India (2001), the Supreme Court interpreted "within the Iddat period" (Section 3(1)(a) of the 1986 Act) to mean:
o: Maintenance is strictly limited to only three months of payment, with nothing more
The TIMING by which the husband must arrange adequate provision for the wife's entire future life — not a limitation on the total amount
The Act was entirely unconstitutional and void
Iddat no longer applies to any Muslim divorce
questions.src: Danial Latifi harmonised the 1986 Act with Shah Bano's substance, interpreting the phrase as a timing requirement, not an amount cap.

questions.q: Following recent developments, a divorced Muslim woman seeking maintenance in India may generally claim under:
o: Only the 1986 Act, with Section 125 CrPC/144 BNSS being unavailable to her
EITHER Section 144 BNSS (formerly Section 125 CrPC) OR the 1986 Act, whichever provides a more favourable outcome
Neither provision applies to Muslim women
Only if she remarries within the Iddat period
questions.src: Current settled position allows a divorced Muslim woman to choose whichever remedy (secular Section 144 BNSS or the 1986 Act) is more favourable.

questions.q: "Hizanat" under Muslim law refers to:
o: Legal guardianship of a minor's property
The right of CUSTODY of a minor child, often vested in the mother for young children
A form of divorce
A type of dower payment
questions.src: Hizanat is specifically the right of custody, distinct from Wilayat (legal guardianship of person/property, typically the father).

questions.q: "Wilayat" under Muslim law, as distinguished from Hizanat, refers to:
o: The same concept as Hizanat, with no real distinction
Legal GUARDIANSHIP of a minor's person/property, typically vested in the father
A form of dower
A type of testamentary bequest
questions.src: Wilayat is legal guardianship (distinct from custody/Hizanat), typically held by the father even where the mother has custody of a young child.

questions.q: Under Muslim law, a bequest by will (Wasiyat) to a NON-HEIR generally cannot exceed what fraction of the testator's net estate, without other heirs' consent?
o: One-half (1/2)
One-third (1/3)
Two-thirds (2/3)
There is no limitation whatsoever
questions.src: The one-third limitation protects the fixed Quranic shares allocated to legal heirs from being defeated by excessive bequests to outsiders.

questions.q: A bequest by will to a person who IS already a legal HEIR under Muslim law is generally:
o: Always automatically valid with no restrictions
Not valid unless the OTHER legal heirs consent to it after the testator's death
Prohibited under all circumstances, even with consent
Only valid if made orally, never in writing
questions.src: Bequests to existing heirs require the consent of the other heirs, since such bequests would otherwise disturb the fixed Quranic distribution shares.

questions.q: Under Sunni law's inheritance scheme, "Sharers" are heirs who:
o: Receive no share whatsoever
Are entitled to FIXED, Quran-specified fractional shares of the estate
Only inherit if there are no other heirs at all
Are limited exclusively to male relatives
questions.src: Sharers receive specific fixed fractional shares as laid down by Quranic principles, distinct from Residuaries who take the remainder.

questions.q: Under Muslim law, a testamentary guardian for minor children may generally be appointed by:
o: Only a court, never the father
The father, by will, to take effect after his death
Only the mother, never the father
No one — testamentary guardianship is not recognised
questions.src: A father may validly appoint a testamentary guardian by will for his minor children, subject to the appointee being fit and proper.

questions.q: The Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937 primarily:
o: Abolished all Muslim personal law in India
Mandated that Muslim Personal Law (not custom) governs specified matters including marriage, dower, and inheritance for Muslims in India
Applied only to Hindu citizens
Was repealed immediately after enactment
questions.src: The 1937 Act established that codified/interpreted Muslim Personal Law, rather than potentially varying local custom, governs these specified matters for Indian Muslims.

questions.q: Under Muslim law, the "Iddat" period observed by a widow after her husband's death is generally:
o: 3 menstrual cycles, same as divorce
4 lunar months and 10 days
Exactly one calendar year
There is no Iddat period for widows
questions.src: The widow's Iddat period (4 lunar months and 10 days) is longer than the standard divorce Iddat period (3 menstrual cycles/months).

questions.q: Under Muslim law, where a husband dies without paying dower owed to his wife, the widow generally has:
o: No remedy whatsoever regarding the unpaid dower
A right to retain possession of the husband's property (lawfully in her possession) until her dower debt is satisfied
The right to automatically inherit the husband's entire estate
Only the right to remarry immediately
questions.src: The widow's right of retention (a form of lien) gives her priority in recovering unpaid dower from property in her possession from the deceased's estate.

questions.q: "Talaq-e-Hasan," as distinguished from Talaq-e-Ahsan, involves:
o: A single pronouncement only
THREE separate pronouncements, one in each successive Tuhr, with the first two revocable and only the third making it final
Pronouncements made entirely in writing with no verbal component
A form recognised only under Shia law
questions.src: Talaq-e-Hasan spreads three pronouncements across three successive Tuhrs, distinct from Ahsan's single pronouncement and Biddat's single-sitting instant form.
